Almost no Indian is below the lowest pov.takeaway: In 2024, 2.3% of Indians were below $3 a day, 15% below $4.20 and 79% below $8.30.
Almost no Indian is below the lowest pov.detail: All three lines come from the same household spending data. The lowest line fell from 49% in 1990 to near zero; the highest was still 93% in 2011 and has fallen since. The gap between them is where most Indians live.
Almost no Indian is below the lowest pov.whyShowThis: It holds the whole answer: both 'poverty has nearly ended' and 'most Indians are poor' are true, at different lines.
Almost no Indian is below the lowest pov.howToRead: Each line is the share of Indians below one poverty line, from 1990. Dots mark survey years. After 2024 the lines are dashed because they are estimates from growth forecasts. The lines are in price-adjusted (PPP) dollars a person a day, not dollars at the exchange rate; the rupee amounts in the key are at 2023-24 prices.
Almost no Indian is below the lowest pov.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the dashed years as measurements. The last survey was 2023-24.
Almost no Indian is below the lowest pov.mobileNote: Look at where the three lines end in 2024: near 2%, near 15% and near 79%.

The world's fall in extreme poverty stal.takeaway: The world's share below $3 a day has been stuck near 10% since about 2019. India's fell to 2.3% by 2024.
The world's fall in extreme poverty stal.detail: India began above the world average in 1990 and is now far below it. Sub-Saharan Africa, where most of the world's extremely poor now live, has stayed near 45% for a decade.
The world's fall in extreme poverty stal.whyShowThis: It puts India's fall in a world where progress has stopped.
The world's fall in extreme poverty stal.howToRead: Three lines, one each for India, the world and Sub-Saharan Africa, show the share below $3 a day. The flat world line after 2019 is the stall.
The world's fall in extreme poverty stal.mistakeToAvoid: India has no usable survey between 2011-12 and 2022-23, so its line through those years is the World Bank's estimate.
The world's fall in extreme poverty stal.mobileNote: Compare where India and the world sit in 2024.

India has 18% of the world's people, 4%.takeaway: India is under-represented among the world's extremely poor and over-represented among everyone below $8.30.
India has 18% of the world's people, 4%.detail: At $3 a day India holds 4% of the world's poor; at $4.20, 15%, the largest group anywhere; at $8.30, 30%. Its share of the world's people is about 18%.
India has 18% of the world's people, 4%.whyShowThis: It shows how India's place in the world changes with the line.
India has 18% of the world's people, 4%.howToRead: Each row is one poverty line. Compare India's share of the world's poor with its share of world population.
India has 18% of the world's people, 4%.mistakeToAvoid: These are shares of the world's poor, not India's poverty rate.
India has 18% of the world's people, 4%.mobileNote: The population bar is the same in every row; watch the poor bar grow.

A 10% fall in spending would push the sh.takeaway: Many Indians sit just above each line. A 10% fall in spending would add about eight in every hundred Indians to those below $4.20 a day.
A 10% fall in spending would push the sh.detail: The World Bank splits India into a thousand equal slices from poorest to richest. Cutting every slice's spending by 10% and counting again shows how many people are within 10% of each line.
A 10% fall in spending would push the sh.whyShowThis: It measures how thin the cushion above each line is.
A 10% fall in spending would push the sh.howToRead: The open dot is 2024. The solid dot is the same population after a 10% fall in everyone's spending. The longer the gap, the more people are close to the line.
A 10% fall in spending would push the sh.mistakeToAvoid: This is a thought experiment, not a forecast of a shock.
A 10% fall in spending would push the sh.mobileNote: The middle row, $4.20, moves the most.

47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.takeaway: Poverty at the middle line is highest in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha, and lowest in Goa, Delhi, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.detail: The share below $4.20 a day ranges from about 47% in Jharkhand to under 3% in Goa. Bihar is at 27% and Uttar Pradesh at 26%.
47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.whyShowThis: It shows where the poor are concentrated.
47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.howToRead: Darker states have a larger share of people below $4.20 a day, about Rs 95.
47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.mistakeToAvoid: A share is not a count. Uttar Pradesh has far more poor people than Jharkhand because it has far more people.
47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.mobileNote: Tap a state to see its share.

In every state, small children are more.takeaway: In all 36 states and union territories, children under six are more likely than the average resident to live below $8.30 a day.
In every state, small children are more.detail: In Kerala it is 75.8% of young children against 58.5% of everyone. A household with small children has more people to feed on the same earnings, so its spending per person is lower.
In every state, small children are more.whyShowThis: It shows who carries the most poverty within each state.
In every state, small children are more.howToRead: In each row, the open dot is everyone and the solid dot is children aged 0 to 5. The solid dot is always further right.
In every state, small children are more.mistakeToAvoid: This measures household spending per person, not what a child eats.
In every state, small children are more.mobileNote: Read the gap between the two dots, not their level.

India has less extreme poverty than Bang.takeaway: India has a smaller share below $3 than Bangladesh, Indonesia or Pakistan, and a larger share below $8.30 than Bangladesh, Indonesia or Viet Nam.
India has less extreme poverty than Bang.detail: In 2024, 2.3% of Indians were below $3 a day, against about 5% in Bangladesh and Indonesia. At $8.30, India's 79% compares with about 68% in both. Viet Nam is at 18%.
India has less extreme poverty than Bang.whyShowThis: It tests India's record against countries with similar histories.
India has less extreme poverty than Bang.howToRead: Each country has three bars, one for each line. Compare the same line across countries.
India has less extreme poverty than Bang.mistakeToAvoid: Only Indonesia's figure comes from a 2024 survey. The rest are estimates for 2024.
India has less extreme poverty than Bang.mobileNote: Compare India's first and last bar with Bangladesh's.

Poor Indians work almost the same hours.takeaway: Paid employees below $3 a day work about 44 hours a week, almost exactly as many as those above it.
Poor Indians work almost the same hours.detail: The self-employed and unpaid workers in poor households work about 37 hours, against 41 in better-off ones. The difference in hours is too small to explain the difference in spending.
Poor Indians work almost the same hours.whyShowThis: It rules out not working enough as the main reason for poverty.
Poor Indians work almost the same hours.howToRead: Each row compares weekly hours for workers in households below and above $3 a day.
Poor Indians work almost the same hours.mistakeToAvoid: Hours, not pay. This chart uses the $3 line.
Poor Indians work almost the same hours.mobileNote: The two dots in each row are close together.

Poor workers are more often self-employe.takeaway: 58% of workers in households below $8.30 a day are self-employed, against 45% above it; 46% work in farming, against 25%.
Poor workers are more often self-employe.detail: Self-employment here usually means a small farm, a cart or a shop counter without a salary. The kind of work, not the amount, separates poor and better-off workers.
Poor workers are more often self-employe.whyShowThis: It points to what differs once hours are ruled out.
Poor workers are more often self-employe.howToRead: The open dot is workers in better-off households, the solid dot workers in poor households.
Poor workers are more often self-employe.mistakeToAvoid: This uses the $8.30 line, unlike the hours chart beside it.
Poor workers are more often self-employe.mobileNote: Both solid dots sit further right.

Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has g.takeaway: By 2024-25, real GDP per person stood at about 162 against 100 in 2014-15. A farm labourer's real wage stood at about 109.
Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has g.detail: A rural non-farm labourer's wage was about 102 and a construction worker's about 98. Factory workers' daily pay reached about 106 by 2023-24. The farm wage grew about 0.8% a year, the same rate Das and Drèze found.
Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has g.whyShowThis: It tests whether economic growth reached the pay of the workers most likely to be poor.
Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has g.howToRead: Every line starts at 100 in 2014-15, the first full year of the Labour Bureau's current occupation list. Prices are taken out with one consumer price index on a single base.
Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has g.mistakeToAvoid: These are wage rates for men, not household incomes. More earners per household can raise spending while wages stay flat.
Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has g.mobileNote: One line climbs; the rest stay near 100.

If poor households had better-off househ.takeaway: Closing the gaps in jobs and pay between poor and better-off households would cut the share below $8.30 a day by about 22 points.
If poor households had better-off househ.detail: The share below $3 a day would halve, from 2.3% to 1.1%. Even so, more than half of Indians would remain below $8.30.
If poor households had better-off househ.whyShowThis: It sizes how much jobs and pay alone could do.
If poor households had better-off househ.howToRead: Each row compares 2024 with the World Bank's simulation for the same measure.
If poor households had better-off househ.mistakeToAvoid: An accounting exercise, not a forecast or a costed policy.
If poor households had better-off househ.mobileNote: Read the first row: 79 now, 57 simulated.

New price data raised India's extreme po.takeaway: On the same 2023-24 survey, the switch to 2021 prices raised extreme poverty from 1.0% to 2.6% and cut the middle-line rate from 19.9% to 16.1%.
New price data raised India's extreme po.detail: The World Bank moved its lines from $2.15, $3.65 and $6.85 to $3, $4.20 and $8.30 in June 2025. The households and their spending did not change; the measuring rule did.
New price data raised India's extreme po.whyShowThis: It shows how a change of yardstick can move a poverty rate overnight.
New price data raised India's extreme po.howToRead: Each row is one line. The open dot is the old price base, the solid dot the new.
New price data raised India's extreme po.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the change as people becoming poorer or richer.
New price data raised India's extreme po.mobileNote: The top two rows move in opposite directions.

Depending on the line and the method, In.takeaway: Published estimates of India's 2022-23 poverty rate run from about 2% to 26%.
Depending on the line and the method, In.detail: The World Bank's direct readings of the new survey sit at the bottom. Estimates that bridge the old and new surveys, on India's own Tendulkar and Rangarajan lines, sit between 11% and 26%.
Depending on the line and the method, In.whyShowThis: It shows how much of the argument is about the line and the method.
Depending on the line and the method, In.howToRead: Each bar is one published estimate. Compare bars that use the same line.
Depending on the line and the method, In.mistakeToAvoid: This is not a margin of error. It mixes different lines and models.
Depending on the line and the method, In.mobileNote: Bars are ordered from highest to lowest.

Between the two newest surveys, the poor.takeaway: From 2022-23 to 2023-24, the poorest tenth's real spending grew about 13%; the richest surveyed tenth's fell about 3%.
Between the two newest surveys, the poor.detail: The average rose about 5%. The World Bank treats these two surveys as comparable with each other, though not with earlier ones.
Between the two newest surveys, the poor.whyShowThis: It shows who gained within the comparable new surveys.
Between the two newest surveys, the poor.howToRead: Each bar is one tenth of the population by spending, poorest at the top.
Between the two newest surveys, the poor.mistakeToAvoid: Part of the jump may be better measurement, the World Bank says; and the survey misses many of the richest households, so this is not evidence that rich Indians became poorer.
Between the two newest surveys, the poor.mobileNote: The bars shrink from top to bottom.

Since 1977, household spending in the na.takeaway: Since 1977, real GDP per person has grown about 5.7 times, household spending in the national accounts about 4.5 times, and spending in the surveys about 2.1 times.
Since 1977, household spending in the na.detail: Part of the gap may be spending the surveys never see, especially among wealthier households. Part comes from how each is defined and valued. Nobody can yet split the gap precisely.
Since 1977, household spending in the na.whyShowThis: It shows why the surveys may understate both spending and inequality.
Since 1977, household spending in the na.howToRead: Each line starts at 100 in 1977. Survey readings are dots; grey links join surveys that are not comparable.
Since 1977, household spending in the na.mistakeToAvoid: The gap does not prove that missing rich households explain all of it.
Since 1977, household spending in the na.mobileNote: Compare where the three lines end.

Money poverty is the smallest of these n.takeaway: 35.5% of young children were stunted and about 31% of Indians faced hardship from health spending, against 5% below $3 a day.
Money poverty is the smallest of these n.detail: The World Bank's measure that adds schooling, water, sanitation and electricity counts 17.7% of Indians as poor on the 2022-23 survey. Each measure covers a different population and year.
Money poverty is the smallest of these n.whyShowThis: It shows what a spending line cannot see.
Money poverty is the smallest of these n.howToRead: Each bar is a separate measure. They overlap and cannot be added.
Money poverty is the smallest of these n.mistakeToAvoid: Stunting is a share of children under five, from 2019-21, not of all Indians.
Money poverty is the smallest of these n.mobileNote: The bottom bar is the spending measure.
